text: Monday, when curried mutton was chosen for supper at the trainer's house
why: ¶218 says Straker and his wife were the only ones who could have chosen curried mutton for supper that night, and the night in question is Monday.

text: Monday evening, when the stable-lad's dish was set aside
why: ¶218 refers to the dish being set aside for the stable-boy, and the maid carried it down on Monday evening.

text: Monday evening, when the opium was added to the stable-lad's dish
why: ¶218 states the opium was added after the dish was set aside for the stable-boy.

text: Who chose curried mutton for supper that Monday night?
why: ¶218 raises this directly: only Straker and his wife could have chosen the curry.

text: How was the opium got into the stable-boy's dish without the maid seeing?
why: ¶218 asks which of them had access to the dish without the maid seeing them.

text: How was the opium got into the stable-boy's dish without the maid seeing? — while the dish stood set aside in the kitchen, before the maid took it

why: This follows from ¶218, which says the opium went in after the dish was set aside and before the maid carried it down.

text: How was the opium got into the stable-boy's dish without the maid seeing? — the maid's attention was drawn away for a moment
id: q.opium_how=the maid's attention was drawn away for a moment
why: A reasonable possibility, given that ¶218 asks how anyone reached the dish unseen by the maid.

text: Did Mrs. Straker know what her husband was about that night?
why: ¶214 calls Straker unworthy of confidence, and ¶218 centres attention on him and his wife, so the reader has reason to wonder about her knowledge.

text: Did Mrs. Straker know what her husband was about that night? — she knew nothing of it
why: A plain possibility answering the open question in label 8.

text: Did Mrs. Straker know what her husband was about that night? — she was in it with him
